text: Chapter 4 has covered policies, standards, naming, lifecycle, and enforcement. This closing lesson covers a big part of why many of those rules exist in the first place: the regulatory landscape.

One important caveat before anything else: this is an orientation to the shape of a few widely-referenced regulations, not legal advice, and not a comprehensive survey of global privacy law. If your organization has real compliance obligations, that needs actual legal counsel — what this lesson gives you is just enough vocabulary to follow why a policy exists.

Three regulations come up constantly. GDPR covers personal data broadly for EU residents, with a generally opt-in consent model. CCPA and its expansion, CPRA, cover California consumers with a generally opt-out model for selling or sharing data. And HIPAA protects health information specifically, inside US healthcare contexts, for covered entities and their business associates.

If you remember one structural fact, make it this: GDPR defaults to opt-in — consent before processing. CCPA defaults to opt-out — it collects by default, and the consumer has to act to stop it. An organization compliant with one of these is not automatically compliant with the other — the mechanics are genuinely different, not just the paperwork.

Regulation is one of the main reasons a policy exists, and one of the main triggers that sends it back through its lifecycle. That closes Chapter 4. Next chapter turns everything so far into an actual governance program, starting with assessing readiness. See you there.
